claim: CDK5RAP2, CEP152, WDR62 and CEP63 colocalize at the centrosome.
source: Primary microcephaly (MCPH) associated proteins CDK5RAP2, CEP152, WDR62 and CEP63 colocalize at the centrosome.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1C showing colocalization of these proteins at centrosomes.

claim: CDK5RAP2, CEP152, WDR62 and CEP63 interact to promote centriole duplication.
source: We found that they interact to promote centriole duplication and form a hierarchy in which each is required to localize another to the centrosome, with CDK5RAP2 at the apex, and CEP152, WDR62 and CEP63 at sequentially lower positions.
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data in Figure 1A and centriole duplication assays in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: MCPH proteins form a hierarchy with CDK5RAP2 at the apex, followed by CEP152, WDR62 and CEP63 at sequentially lower positions.
source: We found that they interact to promote centriole duplication and form a hierarchy in which each is required to localize another to the centrosome, with CDK5RAP2 at the apex, and CEP152, WDR62 and CEP63 at sequentially lower positions.
evidence: Demonstrated by depletion experiments in Figure 1C showing that CDK5RAP2 depletion prevents localization of CEP152, WDR62, and CEP63, while CEP63 depletion does not affect the others.

claim: CDK5RAP2 interacts with centriolar satellite proteins SPAG5 and CEP72.
source: MCPH proteins interact with distinct centriolar satellite proteins; CDK5RAP2 interacts with SPAG5 and CEP72, CEP152 with CEP131, WDR62 with MOONRAKER, and CEP63 with CEP90 and CCDC14.
evidence: Confirmed by mass spectrometry (Supplementary file 1) and co-immunoprecipitation in Figure 3A,B.

claim: CEP152 interacts with centriolar satellite protein CEP131.
source: MCPH proteins interact with distinct centriolar satellite proteins; CDK5RAP2 interacts with SPAG5 and CEP72, CEP152 with CEP131, WDR62 with MOONRAKER, and CEP63 with CEP90 and CCDC14.
evidence: Confirmed by mass spectrometry (Supplementary file 1B) and co-immunoprecipitation in Figure 4A.

claim: WDR62 interacts with centriolar satellite protein MOONRAKER.
source: MCPH proteins interact with distinct centriolar satellite proteins; CDK5RAP2 interacts with SPAG5 and CEP72, CEP152 with CEP131, WDR62 with MOONRAKER, and CEP63 with CEP90 and CCDC14.
evidence: Confirmed by mass spectrometry and co-immunoprecipitation in Figure 5A.

claim: CEP63 interacts with centriolar satellite proteins CEP90 and CCDC14.
source: MCPH proteins interact with distinct centriolar satellite proteins; CDK5RAP2 interacts with SPAG5 and CEP72, CEP152 with CEP131, WDR62 with MOONRAKER, and CEP63 with CEP90 and CCDC14.
evidence: Confirmed by mass spectrometry (Supplementary file 1D) and co-immunoprecipitation in Figures 6A and 7A.

claim: Centriolar satellite proteins localize their cognate MCPH interactors to centrosomes.
source: These satellite proteins localize their cognate MCPH interactors to centrosomes and also promote centriole duplication.
evidence: Demonstrated by depletion experiments showing that loss of satellite proteins prevents centrosomal localization of their MCPH partners (Figures 3D, 4B, 5F, 6B).

claim: Centriolar satellite proteins promote centriole duplication.
source: These satellite proteins localize their cognate MCPH interactors to centrosomes and also promote centriole duplication.
evidence: Shown by centriole counting experiments after satellite protein depletion (Figures 3F-I, 4D-F, 5B-D, 6D-F).

claim: Homozygous mutations in CEP90 may cause MCPH.
source: Consistent with a role for satellites in microcephaly, homozygous mutations in one satellite gene, CEP90, may cause MCPH.
evidence: A homozygous missense variant (p.E89Q) in CEP90 was identified in two affected siblings with microcephaly (Figure 6I,J), and this mutation disrupts CEP90-CEP63 interaction (Figure 6K).

claim: MCPH proteins and satellite proteins (except CCDC14) promote centriole duplication by recruiting CDK2 to the centrosome.
source: The satellite proteins, with the exception of CCDC14, and MCPH proteins promote centriole duplication by recruiting CDK2 to the centrosome.
evidence: Depletion of MCPH proteins and satellite proteins (except CCDC14) reduces CDK2 centrosomal localization (Figure 7—figure supplement 5A,B).

claim: CCDC14 opposes centriole duplication by limiting centrosomal localization of CEP63 and CDK2.
source: In contrast to the other centriolar satellites components that promote MCPH-associated protein localization to the centrosomes and centriole duplication, CCDC14 opposes this pathway by limiting the centrosomal localization of CEP63 and its interactor CDK2.
evidence: CCDC14 depletion causes supernumerary centrioles (Figure 7C) and increased CEP63 and CDK2 at centrosomes (Figures 7D,H).

claim: CDK5RAP2, CEP152, WDR62 and CEP63 co-immunoprecipitate with each other.
source: Consistent with this possibility, co-immunoprecipitation confirmed that CDK5RAP2, CEP152, WDR62 and CEP63 interact with each other, but not with an unrelated centriole component, CP110 (Chen et al., 2002, Figure 1A).
evidence: Shown by co-immunoprecipitation experiments in Figure 1A.

claim: CDK5RAP2, CEP152, WDR62 and CEP63 co-fractionate with the centrosomal protein CP110 in sucrose gradient centrifugation.
source: CDK5RAP2, CEP152, WDR62 and CEP63 co-fractionated with the centrosomal protein CP110 (Figure 1B).
evidence: Demonstrated by sucrose gradient fractionation in Figure 1B.

claim: Depletion of CEP152 disrupts centriole duplication.
source: Consistent with previous studies, depletion of CEP152 or CEP63 disrupted centriole duplication (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,G; Brown et al., 2013).
evidence: Shown by centriole counting in S phase cells after CEP152 depletion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).

claim: Depletion of CEP63 disrupts centriole duplication.
source: Consistent with previous studies, depletion of CEP152 or CEP63 disrupted centriole duplication (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,G; Brown et al., 2013).
evidence: Shown by centriole counting in S phase cells after CEP63 depletion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).

claim: Depletion of CDK5RAP2 inhibits centriole duplication.
source: Similar to the depletion of CEP152 and CEP63, knockdown of CDK5RAP2 or WDR62, inhibited centriole duplication (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,E).
evidence: Shown by centriole counting in S phase cells after CDK5RAP2 depletion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).

claim: Depletion of WDR62 inhibits centriole duplication.
source: Similar to the depletion of CEP152 and CEP63, knockdown of CDK5RAP2 or WDR62, inhibited centriole duplication (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,E).
evidence: Shown by centriole counting in S phase cells after WDR62 depletion (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).

claim: WDR62 localizes to the interphase centrosome.
source: We discovered that, like CDK5RAP2, CEP152, and CEP63, WDR62 localizes to the interphase centrosome (Figure 1C).
evidence: Shown by immunofluorescence in Figure 1C.

claim: WDR62 is present in a toroidal structure with a diameter of 400–500 nm adjacent to SAS6.
source: Also like CDK5RAP2, CEP152, and CEP63, WDR62 is present in a toroidal structure with a diameter of 400–500 nm adjacent to SAS6, a component of the proximal end of procentrioles (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A, Strnad et al., 2007; Sir et al., 2011).
evidence: Demonstrated by structured illumination microscopy in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: CEP152, WDR62, and CEP63 fail to localize to the centrosome in the absence of CDK5RAP2.
source: CEP152, WDR62, and CEP63 failed to localize to the centrosome in the absence of CDK5RAP2 (Figure 1C, and quantitated in Figure 1—figure supplements 2E, 7A).
evidence: Shown by immunofluorescence after CDK5RAP2 depletion in Figure 1C.

claim: Depletion of CEP152, WDR62 or CEP63 has no effect on CDK5RAP2 localization.
source: Conversely, depletion of CEP152, WDR62 or CEP63 had no effect on CDK5RAP2 localization, indicating that CDK5RAP2 has a unique role in localizing other MCPH-associated protein to centrosomes (Figure 1C, and quantitated in Figure 1—figure supplement 6A).
evidence: Shown by immunofluorescence after depletion of CEP152, WDR62, or CEP63 in Figure 1C.

claim: CEP152 is essential for the centrosomal localization of CEP63.
source: CEP152 has previously been shown to be essential for the centrosomal localization of CEP63 (Brown et al., 2013; Lukinavicius et al., 2013).
evidence: Confirmed in this study and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Depletion of CEP152 prevents WDR62 from localizing to the centrosome.
source: We confirmed this finding and extended it by finding that depletion of CEP152 also prevented WDR62 from localizing to the centrosome (Figure 1C, and quantitated in Figure 1—figure supplement 6A).
evidence: Shown by immunofluorescence after CEP152 depletion in Figure 1C.

claim: Only CEP63 fails to localize to the centrosome in the absence of WDR62.
source: Consistent with a hierarchy of MCPH-assocated proteins, only CEP63 failed to localize to the centrosome in the absence of WDR62, while CDK5RAP2, CEP152 and WDR62 all properly localized to centrosomes in the absence of CEP63 (Figure 1C, and quantitated in Figure 1—figure supplement 6A).
evidence: Shown by immunofluorescence after WDR62 depletion in Figure 1C.

claim: CDK5RAP2, CEP152 and WDR62 properly localize to centrosomes in the absence of CEP63.
source: Consistent with a hierarchy of MCPH-assocated proteins, only CEP63 failed to localize to the centrosome in the absence of WDR62, while CDK5RAP2, CEP152 and WDR62 all properly localized to centrosomes in the absence of CEP63 (Figure 1C, and quantitated in Figure 1—figure supplement 6A).
evidence: Shown by immunofluorescence after CEP63 depletion in Figure 1C.

claim: CEP72, SPAG5, CEP131, MNR, CEP90, and CCDC14 colocalize with PCM1 at centriolar satellites throughout the cell cycle.
source: CEP72, SPAG5 CEP131, CEP90, and CCDC14 all colocalize with PCM1 at centriolar satellites throughout the cell cycle (Figure 2A).
evidence: Shown by immunofluorescence in Figure 2A.

claim: CEP72, CEP131, MNR, CEP90 and CCDC14 associate with PCM1.
source: We confirmed previous reports that CEP72, CEP131, MNR, CEP90 and CCDC14 associate with PCM1 (Figure 2B, Kim and Rhee, 2011; Staples et al., 2012; Stowe et al., 2012; Hall et al., 2013; Firat-Karalar et al., 2014).
evidence: Shown by co-immunoprecipitation in Figure 2B.

claim: SPAG5 is a PCM1 interacting protein.
source: In addition, we identified SPAG5 as a PCM1 interacting protein (Figure 2B).
evidence: Shown by co-immunoprecipitation in Figure 2B.

claim: After brief treatment with nocodazole, a portion of CDK5RAP2, CEP152, WDR62 and CEP63 relocalizes to PCM1 aggregates.
source: Like satellite cargo proteins, microtubule depolymerization caused a portion of CDK5RAP2, CEP152, WDR62 and CEP63 to relocalize to PCM1 aggregates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Shown by immunofluorescence after nocodazole treatment in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: γ-tubulin does not accumulate at nocodazole-induced PCM1 aggregates.
source: In contrast, γ-tubulin did not accumulate at the nocodazole-induced PCM1 aggregates, suggesting that not all centrosomal proteins move from centriolar satellites to the centrosome in a microtubule-dependent manner (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Shown by immunofluorescence after nocodazole treatment in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Endogenous CDK5RAP2 protein interacts with CEP72 and SPAG5.
source: We confirmed that the endogenous CDK5RAP2 protein interacts with CEP72 and SPAG5 by reciprocal immunoprecipitation (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: Shown by reciprocal co-immunoprecipitation in Figure 3A,B.

claim: CEP72 and SPAG5 immunoprecipitate each other.
source: In addition to interacting with CDK5RAP2, we found that CEP72 and SPAG5 immunoprecipitated each other (Figure 3C).
evidence: Shown by co-immunoprecipitation in Figure 3C.

claim: CDK5RAP2 fails to localize to the centrosome in CEP72-depleted cells.
source: In HeLa cells depleted of either CEP72 or SPAG5, there was a sharp decrease in the localization of CDK5RAP2 at the centrosome (Figure 3D).
evidence: Shown by immunofluorescence after CEP72 depletion in Figure 3D.

claim: CDK5RAP2 fails to localize to the centrosome in SPAG5-depleted cells.
source: In HeLa cells depleted of either CEP72 or SPAG5, there was a sharp decrease in the localization of CDK5RAP2 at the centrosome (Figure 3D).
evidence: Shown by immunofluorescence after SPAG5 depletion in Figure 3D.

claim: The protein levels of CDK5RAP2 are reduced in CEP72 and SPAG5-depleted cells.
source: We also found that the protein levels of CDK5RAP2 were reduced in CEP72 and SPAG5-depleted cells (Figure 3E).
evidence: Shown by Western blot in Figure 3E.

claim: The stability of CEP72 is reduced in SPAG5-depleted cells.
source: Interestingly, in addition to destabilizing CDK5RAP2, the stability of CEP72 and SPAG5 was reduced in SPAG5 and CEP72-depleted cells, respectively (Figure 3E).
evidence: Shown by Western blot in Figure 3E.

claim: The stability of SPAG5 is reduced in CEP72-depleted cells.
source: Interestingly, in addition to destabilizing CDK5RAP2, the stability of CEP72 and SPAG5 was reduced in SPAG5 and CEP72-depleted cells, respectively (Figure 3E).
evidence: Shown by Western blot in Figure 3E.

claim: Greater than 78% of CEP72-depleted S phase cells have fewer than four centrioles.
source: Similar to the loss of CDK5RAP2, greater than 78% of CEP72-depleted and 83% of SPAG5-depleted S phase cells had fewer than four centrioles, indicating that these proteins may function together with CDK5RAP2 to promote centriole duplication or stability (Figure 3F–I).
evidence: Shown by centriole counting in Figure 3G.

claim: 83% of SPAG5-depleted S phase cells have fewer than four centrioles.
source: Similar to the loss of CDK5RAP2, greater than 78% of CEP72-depleted and 83% of SPAG5-depleted S phase cells had fewer than four centrioles, indicating that these proteins may function together with CDK5RAP2 to promote centriole duplication or stability (Figure 3F–I).
evidence: Shown by centriole counting in Figure 3I.

claim: Depletion of SPAG5 or CEP72 causes CEP152, WDR62 and CEP63 localization to become significantly decreased at S phase centrosomes.
source: Similar to the depletion of CDK5RAP2, depletion of SPAG5 or CEP72 caused CEP152, WDR62 and CEP63 localization to become significantly decreased at S phase centrosomes of both HeLa and U2OS cells (Figure 3—figure supplements 2C, 3A–C).
evidence: Shown by immunofluorescence in Figure 3—figure supplements 2C, 3A.

claim: CEP152 and CEP131 interact.
source: We confirmed that CEP152 and CEP131 interact by reciprocally co-immunprecipitating the endogenous proteins (Figure 4A).
evidence: Shown by reciprocal co-immunoprecipitation in Figure 4A.

claim: CEP152 is greatly reduced at the centrioles in CEP131-depleted cells.
source: Interestingly, CEP152 was greatly reduced at the centrioles in CEP131-depleted cells (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Shown by immunofluorescence after CEP131 depletion in Figure 4B.

claim: The loss of CEP152 from the centrosome of CEP131-depleted cells is not due to destabilization.
source: Unlike the relationship between CDK5RAP2, CEP72 and SPAG5, The loss of CEP152 from the centrosome of CEP131-depleted cells was not due to destabilization, as CEP152 protein levels were unchanged by CEP131 knockdown (Figure 4C).
evidence: Shown by Western blot in Figure 4C.

claim: Greater than 84% of CEP131-depleted cells in S phase fail to properly duplicate their centrioles.
source: Depletion of CEP131 in HeLa cells and examination of Centrin and CEP131 revealed that greater than 84% of CEP131-depleted cells in S phase failed to properly duplicate their centrioles (Figure 4D,F).
evidence: Shown by centriole counting in Figure 4F.

claim: Depletion of CEP131 has no effect on the localization of CDK5RAP2.
source: The depletion of CEP131 had no effect on the localization of CDK5RAP2, consistent with our finding that CEP152 is not required for CDK5RAP2 localization (Figure 4G).
evidence: Shown by immunofluorescence after CEP131 depletion in Figure 4G.

claim: Depletion of CEP131 abrogates the centrosomal localization of WDR62 and CEP63.
source: In addition to CEP152, depletion of CEP131 abrogated the centrosomal localization, but not the stability, of the CEP152-dependent MCPH-associated proteins, WDR62 and CEP63 (Figure 4G and quantitated in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Shown by immunofluorescence after CEP131 depletion in Figure 4G.

claim: MNR and WDR62 interact.
source: We confirmed the interaction between MNR and WDR62 by reciprocal co-immunoprecipitation (Figure 5A).
evidence: Shown by reciprocal co-immunoprecipitation in Figure 5A.

claim: More than 73% of S phase MNR-depleted cells have fewer than four centrioles.
source: Depletion of MNR revealed that more than 73% of S phase cells had fewer than four centrioles (Figure 5D), a phenotype similar to that caused by the depletion of WDR62 or CEP63.
evidence: Shown by centriole counting in Figure 5D.

claim: WDR62 is absent from centrosomes in MNR-depleted cells.
source: Indeed, WDR62 was absent from centrosomes in MNR-depleted cells, indicating MNR is required for the centrosomal localization of WDR62 (Figure 5F).
evidence: Shown by immunofluorescence after MNR depletion in Figure 5F.

claim: Depletion of MNR does not destabilize WDR62.
source: Similar to the relationship between CEP131 and CEP152, depletion of MNR did not destabilize its associated MCPH protein, WDR62 (Figure 5G).
evidence: Shown by Western blot in Figure 5G.

claim: Depletion of MNR does not affect CDK5RAP2 and CEP152 localization to the centrosome.
source: Consistent with a specific role in WDR62 localization, depletion of MNR did not affect CDK5RAP2 and CEP152 localization to the centrosome or its protein stability (Figure 5H and quantified in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Shown by immunofluorescence after MNR depletion in Figure 5H.

claim: CEP63 and CEP90 interact.
source: Reciprocal immunprecipitation of endogenous proteins confirmed the interaction of CEP63 and CEP90 (Figure 6A).
evidence: Shown by reciprocal co-immunoprecipitation in Figure 6A.

claim: CEP63 is absent from the centrosome in CEP90-depleted cells.
source: Indeed, CEP63 was absent from the centrosome in CEP90-depleted cells (Figure 6B and quantified in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A), suggesting that CEP63 localizes to centrioles in a CEP90-dependent manner.
evidence: Shown by immunofluorescence after CEP90 depletion in Figure 6B.

claim: The levels of CEP63 are unchanged upon depletion of CEP90.
source: The levels of CEP63 were unchanged upon depletion of CEP90, indicating that CEP90 is essential for CEP63 centrosomal localization, but not its stability (Figure 6C).
evidence: Shown by Western blot in Figure 6C.

claim: Greater than 78% of S phase CEP90-depleted cells have fewer than four centrioles.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis demonstrated that greater than 78% of S phase CEP90-depleted cells had fewer than four centrioles (Figure 6D–F).
evidence: Shown by centriole counting in Figure 6F.

claim: The centrosomal localization and protein stability of CDK5RAP2, CEP152, and WDR62 are unaltered in CEP90-depleted cells.
source: Immunofluorescence and quantitative analysis of HeLa cells treated with CEP90 siRNA revealed that the centrosomal localization and protein stability of CDK5RAP2, CEP152, and WDR62 were unaltered (Figure 6G and quantified in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Shown by immunofluorescence and Western blot in Figure 6G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A homozygous missense variant in CEP90 (p.E89Q) was identified in two affected male siblings with microcephaly.
source: Both affected boys possess a homozygous missense alteration in the second coding exon of the CEP90 gene (chr13:73366597G>C [hg19]), resulting in p.E89Q (Figure 6J).
evidence: Identified by whole exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing in Figure 6J.

claim: The CEP90 p.E89Q variant has not been detected in dbSNP138, the 1000 Genomes Project, the ESP6500 databases, or >1000 exomes from 467 Middle Eastern families.
source: CEP90 p.E89Q has not been detected in dbSNP138, the 1000 Genomes Project, the ESP6500 databases, or >1000 exomes from 467 Middle Eastern families.
evidence: Based on database searches.

claim: E89 in CEP90 is highly conserved across species.
source: E89 is highly conserved, including 9/9 vertebrate species including Xenopus and zebrafish as well as much more distantly related species (Figure 6—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: Shown by phylogenetic analysis in Figure 6—figure supplement 3D.

claim: CEP90 E89Q interacts efficiently with PCM1 but does not bind CEP63.
source: Interestingly, CEP90 E89Q interacted efficiently with PCM1, but did not bind CEP63 (Figure 6K).
evidence: Shown by co-immunoprecipitation in Figure 6K.

claim: Endogenous CEP63 and CCDC14 interact.
source: We confirmed that endogenous CEP63 and CCDC14 interact using reciprocal coimmunoprecipitations (Figure 7A).
evidence: Shown by reciprocal co-immunoprecipitation in Figure 7A.

claim: Depleting CCDC14 produces supernumerary Centrin foci in S phase U2OS or HeLa cells.
source: Unlike depleting CEP90, depleting CCDC14 produced supernumerary Centrin foci in S phase U2OS or HeLa cells (Figure 7C and data not shown).
evidence: Shown by immunofluorescence after CCDC14 depletion in Figure 7C.

claim: CEP63 localizes to most of the supernumerary Centrin foci in CCDC14-depleted cells.
source: Consistent with these results, CEP63 localized to most of the supernumerary Centrin foci in CCDC14-depleted cells (Figure 7D).
evidence: Shown by immunofluorescence after CCDC14 depletion in Figure 7D.

claim: Protein levels of CEP63 are unchanged in CCDC14-depleted cells.
source: We confirmed by immunoblot that protein levels of CEP63 were unchanged in CCDC14-depleted cells (Figure 7E).
evidence: Shown by Western blot in Figure 7E.

claim: Co-depleting CDK5RAP2, CEP152, WDR62 or CEP63 blocks the formation of supernumary Centrin foci caused by CCDC14 depletion.
source: Quantitation of Centrin foci revealed that, whereas depleting CCDC14 alone caused the formation of supernumary Centrin foci, co-depleting CDK5RAP2, CEP152, WDR62 or CEP63 blocked the formation of supernumary Centrin foci (Figure 7G).
evidence: Shown by centriole counting in Figure 7G.

claim: CDK2 overaccumulates at the Centrin foci in CCDC14-depleted cells.
source: CDK2, which localizes in the vicinity of the centrosome, overaccumulated at the Centrin foci in CCDC14-depleted cells (Figure 7H).
evidence: Shown by immunofluorescence after CCDC14 depletion in Figure 7H.

claim: Blocking CDK2 activity with roscovitine suppresses the formation of supernumerary Centrin foci in CCDC14-depleted cells.
source: Following DMSO treatment, control cells in S phase had two pairs of centrioles while CCDC14-depleted cells had multiple Centrin foci (Figure 7I, left, and Figure 7J). In contrast, CCDC14-depleted cells in S phase treated with roscovitine only contained one pair of centrioles (Figure 7I, right, and Figure 7J).
evidence: Shown by centriole counting after roscovitine treatment in Figure 7I,J.

claim: Depletion of CDK5RAP2, CEP152, WDR62, CEP63, SPAG5, CEP72, CEP131, MNR, or CEP90 reduces CDK2 centrosomal localization.
source: Immunostaining U2OS cells treated with siRNA to CDK5RAP2, CEP152, WDR62, CEP63, SPAG5, CEP72, CEP131, MNR, or CEP90 revealed that all of these MCPH-associated genes and centriolar satellite genes promote the centrosomal localization of CDK2 (Figure 7—figure supplement 5A and quantified in Figure 7—figure supplement 5B).
evidence: Shown by immunofluorescence in Figure 7—figure supplement 5A.

claim: The protein level of CDK2 is unaltered in MCPH and centriolar satellite protein knockdown cells.
source: The protein level of CDK2 was unaltered in these MCPH and centriolar satellite protein knockdown cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 6A).
evidence: Shown by Western blot in Figure 7—figure supplement 6A.

claim: CEP63 interacts with CDK2.
source: CEP63 interacts with Cyclin dependent kinase 2 (CDK2), a cell cycle-dependent kinase that is activated at the onset of S phase and participates in centriole duplication (Dulic et al., 1992; Hinchcliffe et al., 1999; Lacey et al., 1999; Matsumoto et al., 1999; Meraldi et al., 1999; De Boer et al., 2008; Loffler et al., 2011).
evidence: Confirmed by reciprocal immunoprecipitation in Figure 7—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Centriolar satellites transport cargo along microtubules in a dynein-dynactin dependent manner to deliver proteins to the centrosome.
source: Previous studies revealed that centriolar satellites transport cargo along microtubules in a dynein-dynactin dependent manner to deliver proteins to the centrosome (Kubo et al., 1999; Kodani et al., 2010).
evidence: Based on previous studies cited.

claim: Centriole duplication is coupled to the cell cycle preventing under- or over-duplication.
source: Centriole duplication is coupled to the cell cycle preventing under- or over-duplication, either of which can disrupt spindle formation and chromosomal segregation (Hinchcliffe et al., 1999; Lacey et al., 1999; Meraldi et al., 1999; Vidwans et al., 1999; Haase et al., 2001).
evidence: Based on previous studies cited.

claim: Centriolar satellites are 70–100 nm diameter electron dense structures that participate in microtubule-based transport.
source: Within centrosomes, a pair of centrioles are surrounded by pericentriolar material and centriolar satellites, 70–100 nm diameter electron dense structures that participate in microtubule-based transport (Kubo et al., 1999; Dammermann and Merdes, 2002; Kodani et al., 2010).
evidence: Based on previous studies cited.

claim: PCM1 is thought to function in the delivery of proteins to the centrosome.
source: Centriolar satellites contain PCM1, thought to function in the delivery of proteins to the centrosome (Kim et al., 2008; Kodani et al., 2010).
evidence: Based on previous studies cited.

claim: Depletion of PCM1 reduces the centrosomal localization of select proteins.
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, depletion of PCM1 reduces the centrosomal localization of select proteins (Dammermann and Merdes, 2002; Kim et al., 2004, 2008; Kodani et al., 2010).
evidence: Based on previous studies cited.

claim: Altered centriole biogenesis is associated with human developmental growth disorders, such as primordial dwarfism and MCPH.
source: In addition to chromosomal missegregation, altered centriole biogenesis is associated with human developmental growth disorders, such as primordial dwarfism and MCPH (Mochida and Walsh, 2001, 2004; Woods et al., 2005; Griffith et al., 2008; Rauch et al., 2008; Thornton and Woods, 2009).
evidence: Based on previous studies cited.

claim: Many of the genes mutated in MCPH encode centrosomal proteins.
source: Many of the genes mutated in MCPH encode centrosomal proteins (Bond et al., 2005; Zhong et al., 2005; Kumar et al., 2009; Guernsey et al., 2010; Nicholas et al., 2010; Yu et al., 2010; Sir et al., 2011; Lin et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on previous studies cited.

claim: The association of MCPH proteins with the centrosome is evolutionarily conserved with Caenorhabditis elegans.
source: The association of MCPH proteins with the centrosome is evolutionarily conserved with Caenorhabditis elegans (Delattre et al., 2006; Strnad and Gonczy, 2008).
evidence: Based on previous studies cited.

claim: Three MCPH proteins, CEP152, CEP135 and STIL, interact with and promote the centrosomal localization of SAS4.
source: Three MCPH proteins, CEP152, CEP135 and STIL, interact with and promote the centrosomal localization of SAS4 (also known as CPAP or CENPJ) (Strnad and Gonczy, 2008; Cizmecioglu et al., 2010; Dzhindzhev et al., 2010; Sir et al., 2011; Brown et al., 2013; Lin et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on previous studies cited.

claim: Failure to recruit SAS4 can attenuate centriole elongation and duplication.
source: Failure to recruit SAS4 can attenuate centriole elongation and duplication (Schmidt et al., 2009; Comartin et al., 2013; Lin et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on previous studies cited.
